hero.name: Melba Liston
hero.tagline: Trombonist, arranger and composer — the first woman trombonist to play alongside men in the big bands.

blurb.text: Melba Doretta Liston (January 13, 1926 – April 23, 1999) was an American jazz trombonist, arranger, and composer. She was the first woman trombonist to play alongside men in big bands during the 1940s and 1960s, but as her career progressed she became better known as an arranger, particularly in partnership with pianist Randy Weston. Other major artists with whom she worked include Dizzy Gillespie, Billie Holiday, John Coltrane, and Count Basie.

lanes.label: Home
lanes.source: Her interview: born Kansas City 1926, moved to Los Angeles 1937, back in New York 1979, in Los Angeles for the six or seven years before 1996. Jamaica 1973-79 from her Wikipedia article. She moved between Los Angeles and New York more than once between 1948 and 1956 and the interview's dates for those moves conflict, so the bar is left undivided.

lanes.label: Gerald Wilson
lanes.source: Wikipedia: joined 1943, Wilson disbanded 1948. Her interview: joined after a year or so at the Lincoln Theater (which she entered at 16), stayed five or six years.

lanes.label: Dizzy Gillespie
lanes.source: Wikipedia: joined Gillespie's big band 1948; State Department tours 1956 and 1957. Discography: Gillespie releases with her 1955-57.

lanes.label: Billie Holiday
lanes.source: Wikipedia: toured with Billie Holiday (1949). Her interview describes the tour collapsing but gives no year.

lanes.label: Quincy Jones
lanes.source: Wikipedia: Europe with the show Free and Easy, 1959. Discography: The Birth of a Band! (1959) through Newport '61.

lanes.label: Randy Weston
lanes.source: Her interview: met Weston at Birdland in 1956, '56 to '96'. Discography: Little Niles (1958) to Khepera (1998).

lanes.label: Teaching
lanes.source: Wikipedia: invited by the Government of Jamaica in 1973, returned to the U.S. in 1979. Her interview: taught there five or six years.

lanes.label: Own band
lanes.source: Wikipedia: all-women quintet 1958; Melba Liston and Her 'Bones recorded December 1958. Her interview (Bryant, confirmed): started her own group at the beginning of the '80s; the stroke was 1985.

events.event: Born in Kansas City, Missouri; grandparents lived in Kansas City, Kansas, and she grew up between the two.
Went to school in Kansas City, Kansas, staying with her grandfather during the week and her mother at weekends.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · not confirmed by Liston

events.event: Grew up with a player piano at home (the same piano she still owned in 1996); attended Unity church.
Had a radio show in Kansas as a child performer ('I was a little star').
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · Liston confirms

events.event: Saw a trombone and asked her mother to buy it that same day.
events.stated: Transcriber’s summary or transcript header · Liston confirms

events.when: about five months after getting the horn
events.event: Was playing Deep River and Rocking the Cradle of the Deep, learned from the radio; turned her head sideways to reach the far slide positions.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · Liston confirms

events.event: Took two or three lessons from a Kansas City teacher she disliked, then had her mother cancel him.
Moved to California (Los Angeles); grandmother and aunts went first, she and her mother followed four or five months later by train.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · Liston confirms

events.event: Enrolled at McKinley Junior High School; tested for ninth grade but was placed in eighth because of her age.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · Liston confirms

events.event: Her school music teacher wanted to adopt her to send her to special schools; she refused to leave her mother.
Met Minnie Hightower at school and joined Alma Hightower's youth band; practised at the Ross Snyder playground; played alongside Vi Redd and Alice Young.
Travelled with Miss Hightower and the Melodic Dots in the back of a truck to play a fair—her first time on the road.
Photographed with the Hightower band (Minnie Hightower, Vi Redd, Buddy Redd and others).
Attended Jefferson High School briefly and mainly Polytechnic High School, with Minnie Hightower.
Herb Jeffries played the Lincoln; the Lincoln and the white downtown theatres were separate worlds.
Left Hightower, joined the musicians' union and started working in the pit band at the Lincoln Theater.
Bandleader Bardu Ali had her write music for acts that arrived without charts—the start of her writing career; also performed skits with Pigmeat Markham.

events.when: after a year or a year and a half at the Lincoln
events.event: Joined Gerald Wilson's band ('he stole me out of the band'); first job with him at Shepp's Playhouse; worked as copyist and sometime arranger.
Spent 5–6 years (Wilson says 8) with Gerald Wilson; played Chicago and New York, including a show with Jimmie Lunceford and the Apollo, where she sang and played features.
Toured the South with the Wilson band behind Billie Holiday; the tour collapsed and the band was stranded, getting only as far as Kansas City.
Recorded with Count Basie, according to Gerald Wilson.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · not confirmed by Liston

events.event: Recorded with Dexter Gordon, a schoolmate—her first recording and first time playing without written music.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · Liston confirms

events.event: Joined Dizzy Gillespie's big band in New York (with John Coltrane in it); Billy Eckstine told her Dizzy had held the chair empty a week; the band lasted five months and broke up.
Returned to Los Angeles and Gerald Wilson.
Took the Board of Education exam on her own and worked there two or three years (clerical, night school), taking occasional gigs.
Quit, tried playing again, then worked at the Golden State insurance company before quitting to return to music.
Dizzy Gillespie sent for her again; she went back to New York to stay.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · Liston confirms

events.event: In Gillespie's '56 band; some band members resented a woman being sent for from the West Coast until they played her arrangement; stayed until the band broke up.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · Liston confirms

events.event: Met Randy Weston at Birdland while playing with Gillespie; arranged his album with Little Niles—the start of a 40-year partnership ('56 to '96).

State Department tours with Gillespie to the Middle East and South America (and the Far East); wrote a medley of Ellington, Basie and others for the tour; her Annie's Dance arrangement was well received.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · Liston confirms

events.event: Appeared in the films The Ten Commandments and The Prodigal (as Lana Turner's maid).
Arranged Gloria Lynne's album with strings, including her own songs Love, I've Found You and We Never Kissed; was sick on the recording date so Quincy Jones conducted.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · Liston confirms

events.event: Worked for Ray Charles for two or three years.
Recorded as leader (Melba and Her 'Bones); recording arranged by Leonard Feather.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · Liston confirms

events.event: Helped establish youth orchestras—the Pittsburgh Jazz Orchestra (1964), the Harlem Back Street Tour Orchestra, Pratt Institute Youth in Action—writing and directing; also spent two or three years going to Philadelphia.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · Liston confirms

events.event: Arranged Little Niles and Hi-Fly for Randy Weston's Tanjah.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · not confirmed by Liston

events.event: Went to Jamaica with Randy Weston and taught there five or six years; left when the island's leadership changed.
Jamaica jazz festival, with Frank Foster and Dexter Gordon; she was carrying two horns but not playing.
Invited to the Women's Jazz Festival in Kansas City.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · not confirmed by Liston

events.event: Went back to Jamaica to finish the school year, spent about two weeks in St. Lucia, then returned to New York and bought an apartment.
Married Nelson Harris (her second husband); her tune Len Sirrah is his name backwards; they later separated.
Started her own all-women group in New York, toured the East Coast and China, then gradually replaced women with men (Melba Liston and Company, with Budd Johnson and Al Grey).
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · Liston confirms

events.event: Suffered a stroke, causing memory loss and difficulty speaking.
Named an NEA Jazz Master.
Major Holley took her downtown and helped her buy her first computer.
Her trombone was stolen.
Moved to Los Angeles; continued writing only for Randy Weston.
Arranged Randy Weston's Earth Birth (strings; recorded in Montreal), unreleased at the time of the interview.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · Liston confirms

events.event: Her husband died while visiting his mother in South Carolina, a few months before the interview.

events.when: 1996, about a month before the interview
events.event: Susan Slaughter of the International Women's Brass Conference sent her a new trombone.
Interviewed by Clora Bryant at her home in Los Angeles for the Smithsonian Jazz Oral History Program.
events.stated: Stated by Clora Bryant · not confirmed by Liston

events.event: Planned to return to New York for Christmas after six or seven years in Los Angeles.
Died.

voices.intro: Seventeen musicians who spoke of her on tape. Each card opens the passage in the transcript.

cards.name: Slide Hampton
cards.line: learned in dizzy's band how heavy she was
cards.quote: She played really good, and she wrote music that weighs as much as this building.
cards.source: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

cards.name: Mary Lou Williams
cards.line: was urged by her to play again
cards.quote: Melba, I understand, would go back and say, "Man, Lou played some chords and you ought to hear them. They're really great."
cards.note: Williams calls her only “Melba”, and is reporting what she was told.
cards.source: Mary Lou Williams oral history interview

cards.name: Randy Weston
cards.line: relied on her arrangements, even after her stroke
cards.quote: Then I realized that only Melba Liston could do this.
cards.source: Randy Weston — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

cards.name: Clora Bryant
cards.quote: you have been the best, Melba. You’ve been a guiding light for a lot of people, including me
cards.note: Said to Liston, as her interviewer, in 1996.
cards.source: Melba Liston — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

cards.name: Benny Powell
cards.line: played her arrangements in randy's band
cards.quote: Oh, she had a birthday two days ago, Melba Liston. Wonderful woman.
cards.source: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 16, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]

cards.name: Curtis Fuller
cards.line: in quincy's and dizzy's bands with her
cards.quote: Oh yeah, that was a beautiful relationship.
cards.source: Curtis Fuller — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

cards.name: David N. Baker
cards.line: in quincy's trombone section with her
cards.quote: The trombone section was a very, very good section with Åke Persson playing lead, Melba Liston, Curtis Fuller, and myself.
cards.doc: David N. Baker SI-NEA oral history (2)
cards.source: David N. Baker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

cards.name: Quentin "Butter" Jackson
cards.line: played in her band for kim weston
cards.quote: So I went to Atlantic City and played with Melba Liston. She had a band up there, for Kim Weston.

cards.name: Teddy Edwards
cards.line: first met her at shepp's playhouse
cards.quote: Melba Liston was with the band. She was writing and playing her trombone with the band.

cards.name: Abbey Lincoln
cards.line: held her up as a rare exception
cards.quote: It's a rare woman, like Melba Liston, who comes to the music for the music. Rare.
cards.note: Said while dismissing women in jazz generally; Liston is her exception.
cards.source: Abbey Lincoln — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

cards.name: Shirley Horn
cards.quote: Melba, she was a great jazz artist.
cards.second: Oh, it was swinging, but it left a little something to be desired, for me.
cards.source: Shirley Horn — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

cards.name: Al Grey
cards.line: in dizzy gillespie's big band with her
cards.quote: But we had such a tremendous band that every one of those guys who came out of there are stars today, the ones that are left and all like that, and that was like Lee Morgan, Wynton Kelly, and Phil Woods and Melba Liston
cards.source: Al Grey interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995

cards.name: Gerald Wilson
cards.line: in dizzy's 1950 big band with her
cards.quote: That was that and then they had Melba Liston, they had, um Matthew Gee, another trombone player.
cards.source: Gerald Wilson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

cards.name: Toshiko Akiyoshi
cards.line: sat in with dizzy's band including her
cards.quote: Diz had a big band in those days, and Phil Woods was, I think, lead alto, and uh, Melba Liston was playing trombone.
cards.source: Toshiko Akiyoshi — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

cards.name: Joe Williams
cards.line: shared a bathroom with her in st. louis
cards.quote: Snooky and I were roommates and we shared a bathroom with Melba Liston, who had the next, she had like the adjoining door and the bathroom on her side and on our side.
cards.note: Speaking as co-interviewer in Clark Terry’s oral history.
cards.source: Clark Terry interviewed by Joe Williams and Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, May 19, 1995

cards.name: Vi Redd
cards.line: named her among aunt alma's pupils
cards.quote: Melba — Melba Liston, Dexter Gordon took lessons from Aunt Alma.
cards.source: Vi Redd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999

cards.name: Von Freeman
cards.line: cited her among jazz's early women players
cards.quote: And then Melba [Liston] plays the trombone.
cards.source: Von Freeman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

items.q: But other than that, I just loved the instrument. I didn’t need no inspiration.
items.sum: She said apart from hearing Tommy Dorsey on the radio she needed no trombone model: she simply loved the instrument.

items.q: I loved them, but I don’t have anybody – I do it all from my soul, and if it sounds like somebody, well it sounds like somebody. It’s my inspiration. It’s from my soul.
items.sum: She said that though she loved Ellington's arrangements she wrote entirely from her own soul.

items.q: I’m a woman. That’s that.
items.sum: Asked why no major label ever signed her, she answered that she was a woman, and also that she had no manager pushing her.

items.q: But blowing, I don’t think about nothing but the notes.
items.sum: She said that arranging she might think of something, but blowing she thinks of nothing but the notes.

items.q: he would say, “Girl, write the music for it,” and I would write it. So I started writing.
items.sum: She explained that Bardu Ali had her write music for acts that arrived without charts, which is how she started arranging.

items.q: We just had a good band, and we knew it. We knew we had a good band.
items.sum: She rejected the idea that competition with Lunceford drove the Wilson band: they simply had a good band and knew it.

items.q: I thank him very much for sticking with me, because nobody else did.
items.sum: She credited Randy Weston with pulling her out of the stroke by continuing to have her write, saying no one else stuck with her.

items.q: Anybody I write for, because I haven’t had no training, so I have to dig down and do it from there. All my things are challenging.
items.sum: She said every writing job is a challenge because, having had no formal training, she must dig down for it.

items.q: You’ve got to reach down on everything. I have to anywhere. I don’t know where to go until I reach down and find something.
items.sum: She said she has to reach down into herself on everything she writes before she knows where to go.

items.q: I’m going to blow it two or three years from now, I guess, or something, but I’m going to blow it.
items.sum: Asked if she missed playing, she vowed she would play again in two or three years.

items.q: But I have to be the best that I can do. I don’t know if it’s the best.
items.sum: She said her standard was the best she could do, not being the best.

items.q: I’m sorry that I couldn’t talk more.
items.sum: At the end of the interview she apologized that she could not talk more.

items.q: I was born in Kansas City, Missouri, and my grandparents lived in Kansas City, Kansas, so I was between both of them.
items.sum: She said she was born in Kansas City, Missouri, and grew up between there and her grandparents' home in Kansas City, Kansas.

items.q: I think maybe that’s why we moved out here, because she wasn’t getting no business in Kansas.
items.sum: She suggested the family moved to California because her college-educated mother could not get work in Kansas.

items.q: But it had legs on it. It had really big feet – lovely feet on it.
items.sum: She recalled the childhood player piano's big, lovely feet.

items.q: Yeah, and my aunties would dance.
items.sum: She remembered pedalling the player piano while her aunts danced.

items.q: I’ve got a record – I mean a tape with my mother’s voice on there, and she’s talking about when I first got my horn.
items.sum: She said she had a tape of her mother describing the day she got her first trombone.

items.q: I like mathematics, but I used to like to hear things, and I would say “2 - 4 – 6” or something.
items.sum: She described picking out melodies by ear and naming them by scale-degree numbers.

items.q: I was with my grandpa on the back porch, playing the trombone.
items.sum: She said that rather than running with friends she spent her time on the back porch with her grandfather, playing trombone.

items.q: turning my head sideways. I had to do that until I come out here to California.
items.sum: She explained that as a small child she reached the sixth and seventh slide positions by turning her head sideways, until she moved to California.

items.q: I told my mother to cancel him.
items.sum: She said she had her mother cancel a Kansas City trombone teacher she disliked after two or three lessons.

items.q: Anyway, I told him, “No. I want to stay with my mom.”
items.sum: She said she refused her teacher's plan to adopt her in order to send her to special schools, wanting to stay with her mother.

items.q: I was a little star.
items.sum: She summed up her childhood radio show in Kansas as being a little star.

items.q: We rode up and back in a truck in the back seat – I mean the back of a truck. Miss Hightower and the truck driver was up in the front. We made it. I guess that was my first time on the road.
items.sum: She described riding in the back of a truck to play the fair with Miss Hightower's band, her first time on the road.

items.q: Melodic Dots. Miss Hightower and the Melodic Dots. Oh dear.
items.sum: She named the youth band, Miss Hightower and the Melodic Dots.

items.q: Everything. Everything dancers do. Everything horns do. Everything everybody did.
items.sum: She said Alma Hightower taught them everything for the stage, from horns to tap and hula dancing.

items.q: I was reading already.
items.sum: She said she could already read music before Hightower's band.

items.q: I stayed with her until 16 and I joined the union and started to work at the Lincoln Theater. I think she was kind of pissed off with me then. But anyway, that started me on the road to where I am now.
items.sum: She recounted leaving Hightower at 16 to join the union and work at the Lincoln Theater, which annoyed her teacher but launched her career.

items.q: I was writing for bands – 12, 13, 14, 15 pieces, something like that. That was the start of my writing career.
items.sum: She said writing for the 12-to-15-piece Lincoln Theater band was the start of her writing career.

items.q: I wasn’t thrilled about nothing. I just did everything that you could do when you’re on the stage or in the pit band.
items.sum: She said doing comedy skits with Pigmeat Markham was no big thing, since Hightower had trained her for every kind of stage work.

items.q: We had our thing, and then whitey had his thing.
items.sum: She described the segregated Los Angeles entertainment scene: the Lincoln for Black audiences and white venues downtown.

items.q: He says he stole me out of the band.
items.sum: She reported Gerald Wilson's claim that he stole her out of Bardu Ali's band.

items.q: I worked with him. I was saying 5 or 6, but he said 8 years. That’s a long time. We worked everywhere. We worked Chicago, New York, and everything. I was the copyist and sometime I would do the arrangements.
items.sum: She described her years in Gerald Wilson's band as copyist and sometime arranger, working Chicago, New York and elsewhere.

items.q: I don’t think it’s jazz orientation. I’m going back to New York.
items.sum: She said California lacked jazz orientation and announced she was going back to New York.

items.q: Everywhere we went, because they would say, “Let the girl do something.” Gerald said, “Melba, write something up and do it.” So I did what he said.
items.sum: She said audiences wanted the girl featured, so Gerald Wilson had her write a feature for herself.

items.q: But she left and we were stranded on the bus, and Gerald took all the money that we had and gave it to the fellows to get back home, and we just had enought to get us to Kansas City.
items.sum: She recalled the band being stranded on the bus in the South when the Billie Holiday tour collapsed, with Gerald Wilson giving the men money to get home.

items.q: Mainly, though, I would just stay in the background and play the parts, and saxophone and trumpet played the solos, but, like I said, the girl has to do something, so I had to do something once in a while.
items.sum: She said she mostly played section parts while saxophone and trumpet soloed, but as the girl she was expected to feature now and then.

items.q: Billy Eckstine was out front. He said, “…, where you been? We’ve been looking for you. Dizzy’s had the chair empty for a whole week.”
items.sum: She told how she found Gillespie's club by subway and learned from Billy Eckstine that Dizzy had held her chair empty for a week; she had no horn and had to borrow one and a uniform.

items.q: Nothing was scary, or nothing like that. It was just a drag.
items.sum: She said joining Gillespie without her own horn was not scary, just a drag.

items.q: Nobody. I was good at math and all that, so I said, I’m through with this road business.
items.sum: She said she decided on her own to take the Board of Education exam, knowing she would pass, because she was through with the road.

items.q: And I would go – on my lunch thing, I would go in my car and listen to some . . .
items.sum: She recalled spending her lunch breaks at the insurance company listening to music in her car.

items.q: That was the first time I had played without any music. Oh, Lordy. That was terrible.
items.sum: She said the Dexter Gordon date was the first time she had played without written music, and it was terrible.

items.q: No, I wasn’t unhappy. I just – one day I said no. I quit that. Just me and music again.
items.sum: She said she quit the insurance job one day, not out of unhappiness, and went back to music.

items.q: The guys were cool, but the audience, said, “Girl, (murmur murmur).”
items.sum: She said the men in the band accepted her but audiences murmured at a girl on the bandstand.

items.q: Nobody had played no trombone. Nobody.
items.sum: She said no woman had played trombone in such a band before her.

items.q: It’s just a man’s thing. They wouldn’t do that to me, but other girls, they would turn up their nose or something.
items.sum: She called the men's resentment of a woman in the band 'a man's thing,' saying they spared her but not other women.

items.q: He said, “Go on and take one of those arrangements out and see if they can play it.” Two or three bars later, he said, “Now who’s the …”
items.sum: She recalled Gillespie silencing doubters by having the band read one of her arrangements.

items.q: It stopped. Not falling off. It stopped.
items.sum: She corrected Bryant: the band's work did not fall off, it stopped.

items.q: The students I got.
items.sum: She said that what she won over in Jamaica was the students.

items.q: Because the leaders of the whole island dug me, but the school didn’t.
items.sum: She said Jamaica's leaders supported her but the school did not.

items.q: I came on out. But I had enough of it.
items.sum: She said she left Jamaica when its leadership changed, and had had enough.

items.q: Good and bad and all of that stuff, and I was good and bad and all of that stuff.
items.sum: She described her husband, and herself, as good and bad, and said she had meant to leave him several times before she did.

items.q: Two husbands. One of them didn’t last no time, because he was on some stuff or something, but my husband that I – I loved him.
items.sum: She said she had two husbands, one brief and one she loved.

items.q: No. But you get tired or something. It don’t matter too much.
items.sum: She allowed that love was not hard to admit but that people tire of each other.

items.q: He cared, and then he didn’t care, and then I left him, and then he started up again.
items.sum: She summed up her husband's changing devotion.

items.q: No. He was glad for my music.
items.sum: She said her husband did not resent her music but was glad of it.

items.q: He took off all of his clothes. “You can’t do that.” I was trying to get him out of the room, and the baby’s mama come, and I couldn’t say nothing.
items.sum: She told of a bandmate stripping and entering her hotel room in Washington, and his wife arriving and blaming her.

items.q: But anyway, that’s what girls have to go through.
items.sum: She concluded the story of being blamed for a bandmate's advance by saying that is what women have to go through.

items.q: Len Sirrah – that’s the name of one of my tunes is his name backwards. It’s a nice tune too. I’m hoping to do that when I go back to New York.
items.sum: She explained that her tune 'Len Sirrah' is her husband Nelson Harris's name backwards and that she hoped to do it in New York.

items.q: We worked and worked all around New York and then we went to China. I don’t know what town now. But we went over there and then we came back and then I started weeding the girls out and putting some men in their places.
items.sum: She described her women's group working around New York and touring China, after which she gradually replaced women with men.

items.q: I haven’t done anything out here. I came out here when I had the stroke and everything.
items.sum: She said she had done no work in Los Angeles, having come there after her stroke.

items.q: I was conducting and stuff more than playing. I didn’t play very much at that time. When I was in Jamaica, I had two horns, but I wasn’t playing them. I just carried them around with me.
items.sum: She said that before the stroke she was conducting more than playing, and in Jamaica carried two horns she did not play.

items.q: That was just something.
items.sum: She shrugged off her film work as 'just something.'

items.q: You make too much of these . . .
items.sum: She told Bryant she made too much of her film appearances.

items.q: I want to see me.
items.sum: She said she watched for The Prodigal on television because she wanted to see herself.

items.q: I was Lana Turner’s old girl.
items.sum: She summed up her film role as Lana Turner's maid.

items.q: I had the stroke already. I don’t know if I was talking or not then. But he got me and we went downtown and bought the computer.
items.sum: She recalled Major Holley taking her downtown to buy a computer after her stroke, when she may not yet have been talking.

items.q: Not recently or in the last 20 years or something, but before then I think there was some kind of animosity until they got into my arrangements, and they’d say “oo” and they’d start it over again.
items.sum: She said musicians once showed animosity toward her charts until they played a few bars, said 'oo,' and started over.

items.q: Arrangers, we all friends. Ernie Wilkins and all of us real close. I write the soul music, more or less, and they write the swing and bop stuff.
items.sum: She said arrangers were all friends and that she wrote 'the soul music' while others wrote swing and bop.

items.q: Yeah, I wrote for him, but I didn’t write no different. I just wrote from my soul. I just write what I write. If they like it, they like it.
items.sum: She said she wrote for Thelonious Monk as she wrote for anyone, from her soul, take it or leave it.

items.q: Monk is a piano player and he does things with the piano that nobody else does, and I have to leave spaces and stuff for him.
items.sum: She contrasted writing for Monk, for whom she left spaces, with writing for Mingus.

items.q: Yeah, he gives me the song and the changes, and that’s all. But we’ve been together – what? – ’56 to ’96. How many is that? 40 years. He don’t tell me anything.
items.sum: She said Randy Weston gives her only the song and the changes, after forty years together.

items.q: I think about it and think about it and think about it before I write.
items.sum: She described her method: long thought before writing.

items.q: He brought Little Niles and all those things up to the house, and he said, “I think you should write these things for an album for me.” And I wrote them. I think it’s the best thing.
items.sum: She recalled Weston bringing Little Niles and other lead sheets to her and asking her to arrange an album, which she considered the best thing.

items.q: Randy pulled me out of the stroke, so I have to go with him.
items.sum: She said she owed her first loyalty in New York to Randy Weston, who pulled her out of the stroke.

items.q: I haven’t mad no money. So I could make some money now.
items.sum: Asked whether she had fulfilled her dreams, she said she had made no money and could make some now.

items.q: I don’t like the music today, the music that the youngsters are doing today. I’m an old-fashioned broad
items.sum: She said she did not like the young people's music and called herself an old-fashioned broad.

items.q: It’s nothing there. Once in a while a person comes along and has the business and soul and everything, but ordinarily, youngsters don’t have nothing.
items.sum: She said today's young musicians mostly lack soul, with rare exceptions.

items.q: No. They just have to have some soul. That’s all.
items.sum: She said young players need not imitate the old masters; they just need soul.

items.q: I don’t know. They have it or you don’t have it.
items.sum: She said soul cannot be acquired: you have it or you don't.

items.q: But maybe it was good, because I wouldn’t – I don’t know if I was ready for that.
items.sum: She allowed that never having a manager or label contract might have been good, since she might not have been ready.

items.q: I was talking about music. I didn’t talk to no women, nothing about no home life and all of that stuff. I didn’t even know about it. That was a shame, because I should have talked to them.
items.sum: She regretted not talking with women in the countries she toured about their lives.

items.q: Oh yeah. Everywhere except here, the United States.
items.sum: She said her reception was greater everywhere except the United States.

items.q: I did whatever they told me, and that was one of the things that they told me, and it was just another job for me to do. That’s all.
items.sum: She called the tour medley just another job she was told to do.

items.q: I watch you getting thrilled, and then I get a thrill from that.
items.sum: She said she got her thrill from watching Bryant be thrilled by her arrangements.

items.q: I still write like that.
items.sum: She said she still wrote with the dynamic shadings Bryant admired.

items.q: And go anywhere. No, you have to start from scratch.
items.sum: She finished Bryant's teacher's saying: you can't start at the top and go anywhere; you start from scratch.

items.q: I wrote it, so I decided it.
items.sum: She said she decided to sing her own tune because she wrote it.

items.q: It was – when I was writing, I was writing those in matter of days. I can’t write like that no more.
items.sum: She said she once wrote arrangements in days but could not anymore.

items.q: It’s still good.
items.sum: Hearing her Annie's Dance arrangement, she said it was still good.

items.q: The same as I do now. You sit and think about it and think about it and then you start writing it.
items.sum: She described her method: think it through, then write, letting sections interplay as the arrangement leads.

items.q: Oh, boy. If I could do that that now.
items.sum: She wished she could play like that now.

items.q: I’m blowing it every now and then, but I can’t get but two or three notes on the thing.
items.sum: She said she played now and then but could get only two or three notes.

items.q: I have this arm. I don’t know what to do with this. I tried to turn the thing around and blow it like Slide Hampton, and I can’t . . .
items.sum: She described trying to play left-handed like Slide Hampton because of her stroke-weakened arm.

items.q: You always thinking who or where or something.
items.sum: She teased Bryant for always trying to place what a piece reminded her of.

items.q: So I’ve been writing for strings as long as I’ve been writing for horns.
items.sum: She said she had been writing for strings, as on Gloria Lynne's 1959 record, as long as for horns.

items.q: Yeah. I guess so. Not really, but really.
items.sum: Asked whether writing for voice with strings differed from band writing, she said 'Not really, but really.'

items.q: When I write for Dinah – uh. And when I write for Gloria – it’s oo.
items.sum: She characterized the difference between writing for Dinah Washington and Gloria Lynne with sounds: 'uh' and 'oo.'

items.q: I feel like it’s the song, not the singer, makes the difference.
items.sum: She concluded that the song, not the singer, determines how she writes.

items.q: No. I just went on and did whatever they told me to do. But I would like to – I haven’t written for films – just films that doesn’t say anything.
items.sum: She said she never set goals but would like to write for films.

items.q: It doesn’t matter if I do or if I don’t. I think maybe something in New York is waiting on me now.
items.sum: She said writing for film didn't matter much; something in New York was waiting for her.

items.q: Study. Go to school and learn everything that you can in school, and don’t stop there. Get what you can out of school, jamming and everything. It’s about learning and about doing. It’s hard now. It’s still hard for girls
items.sum: Asked for advice to young women musicians, she told them to study, learn everything they can, and keep learning by jamming, adding that it is still hard for girls.

items.q: I don’t get around too much, and I wouldn’t get around if I was able to. I would be back in New York.
items.sum: She said she rarely went out in Los Angeles and would rather be in New York.

items.q: I was afraid to go out and see everybody – anybody, until six months ago or something like that, because . . .
items.sum: She admitted that until about six months earlier she had been afraid to go out and see anyone after the stroke.

items.q: I didn’t want them to gloat over me or something.
items.sum: She explained that she feared people would gloat over her condition.

items.q: Yeah, I got to get on up.
items.sum: She said she had to get up and keep going after the stroke.

items.q: You don’t think. It’s a long time before you can think. You learn how to eat with . . .
items.sum: Asked what she thought after the stroke, she said for a long time one cannot think, and has to relearn how to eat.

items.q: I used to, but maybe I’ll get that back in New York, but I don’t have to go as fast, anyway.
items.sum: She said she might regain her writing speed in New York, but she didn't need to go as fast anyway.

items.q: She said, if you don’t do nothing else, but just sit up and look at it.
items.sum: She quoted Susan Slaughter, who sent her a new trombone, as saying she could at least look at it.

items.q: But I do play it – blow two or three notes on it now and then. But this arm here, I got to get going.
items.sum: She said she played two or three notes on the new horn now and then and had to get her arm going.

items.q: I’m going to get somebody to – not teach me, but sit with me.
items.sum: She said she would find someone in New York, not to teach her but to sit with her, as she relearned the trombone.

items.q: You’ve got to get your things out all over the place, and maybe one or two people will do it, but you don’t – paying is not the – that’s not it.
items.sum: She said what matters is getting her music out widely, not payment.

items.q: I don’t care about the – what do you call them? Peers or something. But my friends – all the guys are my friends. And the girls . . .
items.sum: She said she did not care about peers or critics; all the musicians were her friends.

items.q: they’re having a bitch of a time. We got to get something together for the girls.
items.sum: She said women musicians were having a terrible time and that something had to be organized to get them out front.

items.q: If they’re going to study and do it, do it.
items.sum: Her last advice to young musicians: if you are going to do it, do it.

items.q: That’s all I can say. Don’t get all hung up with nobody other than your music
items.sum: She advised young musicians not to get hung up on anyone but their music.

items.q: I think maybe this song will be my theme song all over – big band, little band, whatever – if I get everybody to play it like that.
items.sum: She closed the interview with Ben Loves Lu, dedicated to her mother and her mother's husband, and said it might become her theme song.

items.q: I met her, and she was thrilled with my playing the trombone and all that. We had a good thing going for many years. We played everywhere.
items.sum: She recalled meeting Minnie Hightower at school and playing everywhere together for years.

items.q: Alice Young. Those three, we were close. I don’t think no other girls were in there at the time.
items.sum: She named Alice Young with Minnie Hightower and Vi Redd as the girls she was close to in the Hightower group.

items.q: I don’t know about that.
items.sum: She deflected Bryant's claim that Miss Hightower thought she was the greatest.

items.q: Sometimes they would work downtown and then come to the Lincoln and do it. It was nice.
items.sum: She said performers would sometimes work the downtown theatres and then come to the Lincoln.

items.q: He said he learned a lot. We just had a good thing going.
items.sum: She said the learning between her and Gerald Wilson went both ways.

items.q: Yeah, behind Lady Day. It was in the South somewhere.
items.sum: She recalled the band backing Billie Holiday on a Southern tour.

items.q: Then I quit that, and I went to playing again, and that didn’t – no, it’s not working. And so I went to work at the insurance company
items.sum: She described quitting the Board of Education, trying music again, and then going to work for an insurance company.

items.q: I went back to New York to stay.
items.sum: She said that when Gillespie sent for her again she went back to New York to stay.

items.q: Gerald, he started it. “She wrote the arrangement. She plays, she sings, and all of that stuff.”
items.sum: She credited Gerald Wilson with introducing her to audiences as arranger, player and singer.

items.q: He was so good. I was there until the band broke up.
items.sum: She said Gillespie was so good and she stayed until the band broke up.

items.q: It was a good thing. He took me to Jamaica. He was there visiting his relatives from there, and I was just hanging out.
items.sum: She said Randy Weston took her to Jamaica, where she was just hanging out at first.

items.q: Oh, I hear from them all the time.
items.sum: She said she still heard from her Jamaican students all the time.

items.q: I bought me an apartment and settled down.
items.sum: She said that back in New York she bought an apartment and settled down.

items.q: When I came out here he used to call me up all the time, and I’m sorry he’s gone.
items.sum: She said her estranged husband kept calling her in Los Angeles and she was sorry he had died.

items.q: Melba Liston and Company, that was all the time. So whatever my company was, that was it
items.sum: She said her group was always called Melba Liston and Company, whoever was in it.

items.q: No trumpets.
items.sum: She told trumpeter Bryant flatly that her group had no trumpets.

items.q: We did, but they didn’t release it or something like that.
items.sum: She said her small group recorded but the recordings were not released.

items.q: I was her maid or something or other. I don’t see it on t.v. or nothing. I’m looking all the time. I’m looking for it.
items.sum: She said she played Lana Turner's maid in The Prodigal and was always watching for it on television.

items.q: He bought my first – the first computer that I had.
items.sum: She said bassist Major Holley bought her first computer.

items.q: It’s always something like a original or one of their tunes, and it’s a great honor – Monk.
items.sum: She said leaders asked her to arrange their own tunes and that writing for Monk was a great honor.

items.q: Sometimes I’m writing for bands that have criteria and then sometimes I’m free to write. Randy, I have all the freedom I want.
items.sum: She said some clients set criteria but with Randy Weston she had complete freedom.

items.q: He says I write like he writes.
items.sum: She reported Randy Weston saying she writes like he does.

items.q: I just want to do that, because she was sending me the horn, so I got to send her something, so I’m sending her one of my compositions.
items.sum: She said she was writing a composition for Susan Slaughter in return for the trombone she was sent.

items.q: Just strings and trumpet and trombone. That’s the first I’ve written for that. I’ve written for trumpet and strings. I hadn’t written for trombone and strings before.
items.sum: She said the new piece was her first for trombone with strings.

items.q: He stayed over and met me when I finished the gig. He said, “I have to meet her.” We just hit it off right away.
items.sum: She recounted meeting Randy Weston at Birdland while playing with Gillespie.

items.q: all the things with three horns or more, I wrote.
items.sum: She said she arranged everything of Weston's with three or more horns.

items.q: What is the fusion?
items.sum: She asked Bryant what fusion was.

items.q: I can’t say all the musicians that came down – once in a while – and played for my kids and the school, and some of those got soul. It’s nothing I can put my finger on.
items.sum: She recalled Dexter Gordon, Elvin Jones and others coming to Jamaica to play for her students.

items.q: I wrote and I directed. Maybe sometimes they were just coming along with their instruments.
items.sum: She said she wrote for and directed youth orchestras in Pittsburgh, Washington and Philadelphia, helping beginners with chords and scales.

items.q: I know, but I had the girls first, and we went all over the East Coast, and we went to China and came back.
items.sum: She insisted her group started as an all-women band that toured the East Coast and China.

items.q: I don’t know how I did them, but it was just me, and I don’t like them today. I don’t know if the tempos are wrong or something.
items.sum: She said she was dissatisfied with some tunes on her record, especially pop numbers she had to do.

items.q: Nobody.
items.sum: She said nobody had ever managed her.

items.q: Almost everywhere I got acceptance. My applause and everything was always great, over there and here and everywhere
items.sum: She said she was accepted and applauded everywhere on tour, even where local women were restricted.

items.q: We weren’t no – I wasn’t doing any politics.
items.sum: She denied any part in the politics of the State Department tour.

items.q: I didn’t know that Dizzy was doing everything that he was doing to keep us together and all that.
items.sum: She said she had not realized how much Gillespie did to keep the band together.

items.q: I mean, I played with all of them, so it was nothing for me to take a little bit of this and a little bit of that.
items.sum: She said assembling a medley of Ellington, Basie and others for the tour was easy because she had played with all of them.

items.q: I think we were – I was supposed to marry him, but he died over there in Canada or somewhere.
items.sum: She said she had been supposed to marry pianist Wynton Kelly before he died.

items.q: No. Nobody gave me no problems. I didn’t have no problems, because they didn’t give me no problems.
items.sum: She said none of the stars she wrote for, including Ray Charles, for whom she worked two or three years, gave her trouble.

items.q: Sometimes.
items.sum: Asked if she got thrilled hearing her arrangements, she said 'Sometimes.'

items.q: I used to. Yeah. Now it’s that electric thing over there.
items.sum: She said she used to compose at the piano and now used an electric keyboard.

items.q: Oh, yeah. But that was the very end. I was busy trying to lay – tell them what the notes were and all of that. But they got it.
items.sum: She said she taught shadings to her Jamaican students only at the end, after the basics, but they got it.

items.q: I write almost straight through and then I go over it and then no telling what happens.
items.sum: She said she writes nearly straight through and then revises, sometimes repeatedly.

items.q: I got to be thinking about the notes, man. I got to be thinking about the notes – the notes, man.
items.sum: She said that while playing she has to be thinking about the notes.

items.q: But it’s not that much different. It’s the same thing as far as I’m concerned.
items.sum: She said her strings version of Little Niles was not that different from her original.

items.q: Randy tells me how many choruses he’s going to take and where violins come in, but nothing else.
items.sum: She said Weston told her only how many choruses he would take and where the violins came in.

items.q: A high voice or a low voice or a in-between voice and all of those things, but then you just go on and write.
items.sum: She said writing for a singer means considering the voice's range, then just writing.

items.q: Yeah, and I was sick, and the day of the recording date, I was out of it, so I called Quincy [Jones] and he conducted for me, but all of the arrangements are mine – almost all of them.
items.sum: She said she was sick on Gloria Lynne's recording date, so Quincy Jones conducted, but the arrangements were hers.

items.q: But wherever they go to school, college and stuff, make them teach you as much as they know how. And go on, like we did at nighttime – go to other places and get some knowledge there.
items.sum: She advised students to make their schools teach them everything and to seek knowledge elsewhere at night, as her generation did.

items.q: Horn players, get someone to take a pattern off of.
items.sum: She advised young players to pattern themselves on an older musician they like.

items.q: Yeah. Back there. In the West Indies, St. Lucia, everywhere but here.
items.sum: She said young people wanted to learn everywhere she taught except Los Angeles.

items.q: I’ve been here six, seven years or something. I’m going to go back there and get a new start or something.
items.sum: She said after six or seven years in Los Angeles she would return to New York for a new start.

items.q: Oh yeah, but Randy helped me to get started writing, and so I’m doing it. I’m not writing as fast and all of that as I . . .
items.sum: She said her mother pushed her too, but Weston got her writing again, though slower than before.

items.q: No. The horn was stolen.
items.sum: She said she didn't think about not playing after the stroke because her horn had been stolen.

items.q: Yeah, I guess so. Another phase of it, anyway.
items.sum: She agreed that New York would be another phase.

items.q: I don’t think they want to. But anyway, I may be wrong.
items.sum: She doubted young women want to understand what her generation went through, allowing she might be wrong.

items.q: Now and then a girl comes along.
items.sum: She said a good woman player comes along now and then.
